## Overview

We have seen in this course how container images provide a way to make your
software reproducible. How can you  ensure it is also FAIR (Findable,
Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable), secure and maintainable?
In this lesson we discuss some good practices for developing containerised
research software. 

<!-- A checklist is included at the end which can be used to evaluate your own project.-->


## Metadata and provenance

A large portion of FAIR concerns having high-quality metadata, which is information that
describes your software and its associations. For container images, this
means clear tags, plus labels recording details such as authorship and licence.

::: {.callout-tip collapse=true}
## Findable first

Publishing an image on a public, searchable registry such as `ghcr.io`
is the most important step towards findability. You should also link the image
(a 'package' on GitHub) to the public repository containing its source code.
This happens automatically if the image is built and published by a workflow in that repository, as we saw
earlier in this module ([GitHub Workflows](workflows.qmd)), but can also be done 
manually if pushing directly from Podman Desktop (see
[Module 2](../02-building-and-publishing/publishing.qmd)).
:::

### Tags and labels

So far, our `podman.yml` workflow creates an image with a `latest` tag. This
indicates the most recent build  but conveys no version information.
 We can improve this by passing the version in as a parameter when running the
 workflow.

First, add an *input* under `workflow_dispatch` in the workflow:

```yaml
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      version:
        description: Semantic version for the image tag (e.g. 0.0.1)
        type: string
        required: true
```

This can then be used in a build step such as:

```yaml
      - name: Build image
        env:
          VERSION: ${{ inputs.version }}
        run: |
          podman build \
            --build-arg VERSION="$VERSION" \
            --build-arg REVISION="$GITHUB_SHA" \
            -t python-demo:"$VERSION" \
            -t python-demo:sha-"${GITHUB_SHA::7}" \
            -t python-demo:latest .
```
Here we add the version as a tag, but also a tag with the Git commit hash (SHA) via the
`GITHUB_SHA` variable, which
identifies the exact state of the repository when the workflow is run.
As a reminder, multiple tags can refer to the same version of an image.

Second, the `--build-arg` options make the
variables available inside the
`Containerfile`, where they can be used to set labels
automatically:

```dockerfile
ARG VERSION
ARG REVISION
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.version="${VERSION}"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.revision="${REVISION}"
```
You can update the `version` label and add the `revision` label to your `Containerfile`
now and rebuild using the 'Build Container Image' workflow. Note to resolve correctly the `ARG` lines must exist and must come after the `FROM`
instruction that pulls in the base image.

Each image will now have three tags: with different jobs:

| Tag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0.0.1` | A named release |
| `sha-1a2b3c4` | The exact commit it was built from |
| `latest` | The newest build (unreliable) |

::: {.callout-tip collapse=true}
## GitHub Releases
Releases are a GitHub-native way of identifying software versions on GitHub,
appearing under a separate *Releases* tab of a repository. While beyond the
scope of this course, release tags can also be used inside workflows to label
container images. Refer to GitHub's [About
releases](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/about-releases)
documentation if you want to use this feature.
:::

### Licence and citation
You will have noticed that GitHub offers to add a licence file, `LICENSE`, when
you create a repository. This is good practice, as it informs others how they may
use and reproduce your software. Choose a permissive licence if possible: MIT
and Apache 2.0 are amongst the most popular. If you want modified versions to stay open
under the same terms, known as  'copyleft' policy, consider GNU GPLv3. GitHub's
[choosealicense.com](https://choosealicense.com/licenses/) has additional
details and licence text you can copy. Note when adding a `LICENSE` file to your
repository, set the `org.opencontainers.image.licenses` label in your `Containerfile` to
match.

Be aware that your dependencies have their own licences which, for example,
may require you to state any modifications you have made, or release your software
under the same licence. There may also be restrictions for commercial or
large organisational use; make sure to highlight any in your `README.md`.

In addition to licensing, you will probably want to make your software citable. There
are three common ways, which can be combined:

* Add a `CITATION.cff` file to your repository. GitHub will then show a "Cite
  this repository" button (see
  [About CITATION files](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-citation-files)).
* Include a BibTeX entry in a 'How to cite' section of
  the `README.md`, which can be directly copied to a citation manager or LaTeX
  document
* Archive a release of your repository on a service such as Zenodo. This gives
  a permanent DOI to reference in a paper or other work.

## Documentation

Helpful documentation is essential for the accessibility of software.
It can also improve findability given it is likely to be returned
by search engines and AI agents looking for software online. 

### Supporting documentation

As a minimum, your repository should include a `README.md` alongside the `Containerfile`.
This should give  a brief description of the software and usage
instructions, such as required parameters and available command line
arguments. If you provide examples, include a specific version tag
rather than `latest`, in case the usage behaviour changes over time.

::: {.callout-tip collapse=true}
## Self-documenting software

When developing software, consider adding a `--help` option so users can discover
how to use it without leaving the terminal. For Python, the `argparse`
and `click` modules can be used to generate help text automatically from argument
definitions.
:::


### Guidance for contributors

If you would like others to contribute to the development or maintenance 
of your software, a `CONTRIBUTING.md` file will
be scanned by GitHub to create a 'Contributing' tab,
allowing you to explain, how to report a problem, propose a change
or request a new feature.

See GitHub's information on
[setting guidelines for repository contributors](https://docs.github.com/en/communities/setting-up-your-project-for-healthy-contributions/setting-guidelines-for-repository-contributors).

### User manual

Online documentation can greatly increase the reach and usability of your
software. It is most useful for software beyond basic scripts, where
explanations of usage and features cannot sensibly fit into a single
`README.md`.

GitHub Pages offers free hosting for
documentation attached to a repository. Tools such as
[Zensical](https://zensical.org/) and [Quarto](https://quarto.org/) 
turn a set of Markdown files into a website, and can be run
in a GitHub workflow to publish it automatically. Both can also be run from a
container, so you can build and preview your documentation without installing
anything, using the skills from this course. Quarto was used to write these
notes!

<!-- Another popular option is [Read the Docs](https://about.readthedocs.com/), which hosts documentation built from your repository.-->

## Interoperability and reusable design

*Interoperable* software can be used with other software tools and systems,
whilst *reusable* software can be rebuilt and extended by others. 
Podman builds images to the Open Container Initiative (OCI) standard, which
other runtimes such as Docker and Apptainer can read. You get this broad
compatibility, and support across all major operating systems and platforms,
simply by using containers to distribute your software. There are aspects,
however, that you control with the design of your software that determine
how readily others can integrate your software and rebuild it for their own purpose. 

### Input: arguments and data

Most computational work in science comes down to parsing input to a program and
collecting the outputs. 

In Podman Desktop, input parameters and options can be passed by
by setting the *Command* when creating a container. For example, if we adapted
our `python-demo` script to accept a `samples` parameter for the number of
samples in the simulations, a valid *Command* could be
```bash
python script.py --samples 9999
```

If your image does have an entrypoint script, as we introduced in
[Testing Containers](testing.qmd), document its behaviour in the `README.md`.
The simplest approach is to end the script with:

```bash
exec "$@"
```

As explained in that lesson, `"$@"` stands for all arguments passed 
to the entrypoint, which is the contents of *Command*. 
Ending with this line ensures that, once any preparation has
been performed, the desired container command is executed, including any
arguments provided by the user.

The other critical input is data. Aside from small test or sample datasets,
raw data should not be included in the image. Instead, they should be provided at runtime through a bind mount,
set in the *Volumes* section of Podman Desktop when creating a container.
Choose a clear location where your application expects data, e.g., `/data`, and document it.
A common choice is to set `WORKDIR` (see [Module 2](../02-building-and-publishing/index.qmd)) to that
location at the end of the `Containerfile`:

```dockerfile
WORKDIR /data
```

Your script then runs there, reads any data the user has mounted to that path,
and writes new or modified data back to it.

### Output formats

The `python-demo` application only prints a result. This is fragile and not
machine readable. A better option would be to 
create structured output, such as with JSON:
```python
import json
print(json.dumps({"pi_estimate": estimate, "samples": samples}))
```
You could also give users the option to have the script write this to a file
directly.

In addition, it is also a good idea to make use of exit codes. In Python,
the simplest approach is `sys.exit(1)` for a failure and 
`sys.exit(0)` for a successful run. This allows your script to be used in
pipelines where other programs or operations run conditionally on its
success. 

### Easy rebuilds

In [Module 2/Reproducible Builds](../02-building-and-publishing/reproducible-builds.qmd) we advised caution in applying
version pins to system packages and libraries your software depends on. 
Strict pins can make a rebuild fail and block new features being available. 
They also stop your
image receiving security patches for its dependencies.

There are further ways to may your software easier to rebuild and work
with:

- Use `ARG` to parameterise build variants, for example the version of a
  dependency that may affect reproducibility or compatibility
- Follow good programming conventions for your language, such as Python's PEP 8
- Consider how it may be deployed when writing the `Containerfile`. Will people
  want to run it as a persistent background service, or access a web interface
  in a browser?

Together with contributing guidelines and an open licence, these make it more
likely that others will extend your software. Like good science, good software
should encourage others to develop it further.

::: {.callout-tip collapse=true}
## Image layers

For larger applications, how you order the steps in your `Containerfile` affects
build speed, and you can organise the installation into different stages that
can be selectively used by other images. Generally, you want to put components
that you will change often, such as your application code, near the end of the build;
see
Docker's guide to
[understanding image layers](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/building-images/understanding-image-layers/).
:::

## Maintenance and security

Reproducibility and maintainability sometimes feel opposed: strict
reproducibility requires pinning versions of all dependencies, but doing so
can make it very difficult to rebuild or resolve bugs in your software.
As explained aboe, we advise avoiding
pins in your `Containerfile` for system packages and libraries, and only
using them for dependencies your application directly depends on, e.g.,
Python packages. This keeps your software rebuildable and up to date, while
older images can be accessed by tag if a particular revision is required for
reproducibility.

The workflows covered in this module make it easy to rebuild often. Doing so
allows you to catch problems in the build process before they accumulate. Likewise,
automated tests helps ensure the software itself continues to function correctly.

### Setting user
By default, processes inside a container run as the root user (UID=0)
which, in many Docker and some Podman installations, maps to root *outside* the
container. This is a security risk because, although containers should keep
container processes isolated, *if* a bug allows processes to escape, those
processes will have administrative privileges on your computer. Is it therefore
good practice to specify processes to run as a non-privileged user 
in your `Containerfile`. This is achieved with the
`USER` instruction. For example,
```dockerfile
USER 1001:1001
```
sets the UID and GID (user and group-id) to 1001, which should not have any
special capabilities.

## Test your understanding

Try these questions before opening the answers.

1. Your workflow builds only a `latest` tag. Why is this a problem for someone trying to reproduce your results?
2. What are common ways to make it easier for people to cite your software?
3. What is the container specification used by Docker and Podman?
4. How should data be passed to a running container?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse=true}
## Answers

1. `latest` changes with each build and does not indicate which version produced a result
2. Add a `CITATION.cff` file or include citation information in the `README.md`
3. The Open Container Initiative (OCI) standard
4. Via a bind mount, set under *Volumes* in Podman Desktop, to a location inside the container filesystem that your `README.md` documents
:::
